sections.heading: Standing Seam Metal Roofing and Other Metal Roofing Styles

runs.v: starts with the building. Standing seam metal roofing suits long commercial runs and visible roofs, corrugated metal panels are budget-friendly and suitable for industrial settings, and metal shingles mimic traditional roofing materials while offering high wind resistance. Galvalume steel roofing combines aluminum and zinc in its coating for durability, aluminum metal roofs are lightweight and corrosion-resistant, and copper metal roofs can last over 70 years while weathering to a patina whose beauty suits period architecture. Because these metals resist corrosion, metal roofs suit wet climates, although scratched or cut steel can still rust.

c.v: The advantages of a metal roof

runs.v: over other roofing materials are durability, longevity, and low maintenance: metal roofing can last 40 to 70 years, roughly twice as long as asphalt shingles at 20 to 30 years, and it requires minimal maintenance over its lifespan. Metal roofs are resistant to fire and impact damage, and metal roofs can reflect solar energy, reducing cooling costs and improving energy efficiency. Those benefits protect the building and the business inside it for decades, which is why many commercial roofing owners and homeowners choose metal for a new roof.

sections.heading: What Is the Biggest Problem With Metal Roofs?

runs.v: are the biggest problem with metal roofs, because exposed fasteners back out and their washer seals deteriorate as the panels expand and contract, and seams open where thermal movement was not engineered into the clip system. Rust at scratches and cut edges on coated steel, galvanic corrosion where copper meets steel or aluminum, and dents from hail on thinner-gauge or softer panels come next, while rain noise depends on the deck and insulation under the panels. Regular maintenance, including inspecting the fasteners, sealants, and flashing, keeps those problems small and helps maintain the performance of a metal roof for the rest of its service life.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a commercial metal roof in Montclair, NJ?

runs.v: Yes, once roof work on a commercial, multi-family, or attached building exceeds 25% of the total roof area in a 12-month period, per N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and the NJ Uniform Construction Code, and a full metal roof replacement crosses that line; confirm the filing with the Township of Montclair construction office before work begins. With about 46% of Montclair homes in multi-unit buildings, plus the storefronts, much of the commercial work falls on the permit side, while a detached one- or two-family reroof counts as ordinary maintenance.

faqs.q: Does a metal roof in a Montclair historic district need extra approval?

runs.v: It can. A property in a historic district, or a designated landmark, can need extra review before appearance-changing exterior roofing, separate from the building permit, so confirm the parcel's status with the Township of Montclair before work begins. Per the National Park Service, National Register listing alone places no federal restriction on a private owner.

faqs.q: What is the difference between standing-seam and exposed-fastener commercial metal roofing?

runs.v: Standing-seam metal conceals the fasteners beneath the raised seam; exposed-fastener metal drives screws through the panel surface at lower cost and fails first at backed-out fasteners and washer-seal deterioration, per This Old House and metal-roofing industry consensus.

faqs.q: Should you repair or replace a commercial metal roof?

runs.v: Repair it when the damage stays localized; replace a standing-seam roof when seam-connection damage exceeds 25% or panel corrosion exceeds 20%, and an exposed-fastener roof when 15 to 20% of fasteners corrode or panel corrosion exceeds 25%, per metal-roofing industry consensus and HomeAdvisor. That is the 25% rule for roofing in practice: once damage passes about a quarter of the roof, replacement usually beats repair, and recurring leaks in the same spot signal a systemic defect regardless of percentage.
